prompt: Write an essay arguing whether students should be allowed to retake exams until they pass.
text:
# Should Students Be Allowed to Retake Exams Until They Pass?

Students should be allowed to retake exams until they pass, with some sensible limits. The purpose of a course is to teach students something. An exam is meant to show whether that happened. If a student has learned the material by the third attempt, the exam has done its job, and the grade should say so.

## The case for unlimited retakes

A single exam measures a student on one day. It captures how well they slept, whether they were sick, and how anxious they felt, along with what they know. A student who fails once and then studies hard to pass has learned something real. Punishing them forever for the first result mistakes a snapshot for a verdict.

Retakes also change what students do after failing. Under a one-shot system, a failed exam is the end of the matter, and the student moves on to the next unit with a gap in their knowledge. Those gaps pile up. A student who never really understood fractions will struggle with algebra, and one who skipped the basics of anatomy will struggle in clinical work. When students must retake until they pass, the gap gets closed before the next layer is built on it.

Many fields already work this way. People can retake a driving test until they pass. Aspiring lawyers and nurses can retake licensing exams. No one argues that a driver who passed on the fourth try is less safe than one who passed on the first. We care that they can now drive. Schools that insist on one attempt are applying a stricter standard than the professions their students are heading into.

Retakes can also help fairness. Students with unstable home lives, jobs, or health problems are the most likely to have one disastrous exam day. A policy of one chance falls hardest on them. Allowing another attempt gives them room to show what they know without relying on the luck of a good day.

## The objections

The strongest objection is that unlimited retakes cost teachers too much time. Writing, proctoring and grading new versions of every exam is real work. This is a practical problem, and it can be handled. Question banks can generate new versions automatically, and many tests can be graded by software. Schools can also put a short waiting period between attempts, so that grading demand stays manageable.

A second objection is that retakes teach students to put off studying. If you can always try again, why prepare for the first attempt? There is some truth here. But a student who fails still has to spend the time to study and sit the exam again, and that costs more than preparing the first time. Few students would choose that on purpose. Policies can also strengthen the incentive: require a review session or a short study plan before each new attempt, so a retake is earned rather than automatic.

A third objection is that grades will lose their meaning if everyone eventually passes. This depends on what grades are for. If a grade is meant to rank students against each other, then retakes blur the ranking. If it is meant to certify that a student mastered the material, then a pass after several tries says exactly that. I think the second purpose is the better one for education. Ranking people is a side effect, and learning is the goal. Schools can still distinguish levels of achievement, for example by recording the number of attempts or capping the top grade on a retake.

## A reasonable version of the policy

"Until they pass" should not mean "with no structure at all." A good policy would include:

- A short gap between attempts, so students have time to study the material they missed.
- New questions on each attempt, so students cannot just memorize an answer key.
- Required remediation, such as a review session or tutoring, before a retake.
- A clear record of how many attempts were needed, for cases where that matters.

With these in place, most of the practical objections disappear, and the core benefit stays: no student is stopped by a single bad day.

## Conclusion

Exams should serve learning, not replace it. A system that lets students try again until they pass treats failure as information to act on, not a final judgment. It asks students to do the work of mastering the material, and it keeps a bad day from erasing that work. The costs to teachers and the risk of complacency are real, but careful design can manage both. Schools should let students retake exams until they pass.
